title: Co-culture Protocol for Human Cancer and Endothelial Cells
author: Guo, Miller, et al.
materials: FITC Goat Polyclonal Ab to GFP
DOWSIL™ Sylgard 184 Silicone Elastomer Curing Agent

steps.title: Transfer plate and wash rings
steps.instruction: Remove the 24‑well plate containing PDMS rings from the incubator, place it on the bench, aspirate media with a vacuum aspirator (tube tip touching the well wall) and wash each ring twice with ~500 µL PBS for 5 min each on an orbital shaker at room temperature (22 °C–27 °C); ensure the vacuum flask contains 10 % bleach.

steps.title: Fix rings with formalin
steps.instruction: Add ~300 µL of 10 % formalin to each well, incubate 20 min on an orbital shaker at room temperature (22 °C–27 °C), then remove the formalin by pipette and dispose of it as hazardous waste; quenching is not required.

steps.title: Wash and store post‑fixation
steps.instruction: Wash the rings three times with PBS on the orbital shaker at room temperature (22 °C–27 °C), 5 min each. Optionally wrap the 24‑well plate in aluminum foil and store at 4 °C for up to 3–4 weeks before staining.

steps.title: Prepare 2 % BSA blocking buffer
steps.instruction: Dissolve 2 g BSA powder in 100 mL PBS containing 0.1 % Tween‑20 to make a 2 % BSA blocking buffer; incubate at 37 °C for ~20 min to speed dissolution.

steps.title: Block nonspecific binding
steps.instruction: Remove PBS, add 200 µL blocking buffer to each well, and incubate 1 h at room temperature (22 °C–27 °C) on the orbital shaker.

steps.title: Incubate with primary antibody
steps.instruction: Aspirate the blocking buffer, add 200 µL of primary antibody diluted in blocking buffer (according to each antibody’s recommended dilution), wrap the plate in aluminum foil and incubate overnight (12–24 h) at 4 °C on the orbital shaker; multiple primary antibodies of different host species may be combined.

steps.title: Wash after primary incubation
steps.instruction: Remove the primary antibody solution and wash the rings four times with PBST (1× PBS + 0.1 % Tween‑20) for 20 min each on the orbital shaker at room temperature (22 °C–27 °C).

steps.title: Incubate with secondary antibody
steps.instruction: Add 200 µL per well of secondary antibody diluted in blocking buffer, verify correct dilution, species compatibility, and fluorophore selection, then wrap the plate in aluminum foil and incubate overnight (12–24 h) at 4 °C on the orbital shaker.

steps.title: Wash after secondary incubation
steps.instruction: Remove the secondary antibody solution and wash the rings four times with PBST for 20 min each on the orbital shaker at room temperature (22 °C–27 °C).

steps.title: Stain nuclei with DAPI
steps.instruction: Add DAPI solution (prepared at the manufacturer‑recommended dilution) to each well and incubate 20–30 min at room temperature (22 °C–27 °C) on the orbital shaker.

steps.title: Remove excess DAPI
steps.instruction: Discard the DAPI solution and wash the rings at least once with PBST for a minimum of 5 min at room temperature to remove excess DAPI.

steps.title: Image stained rings
steps.instruction: Acquire fluorescence images of the rings on an inverted fluorescence microscope; after imaging, wrap the plate in aluminum foil and store at 4 °C for 4–6 weeks if needed.

steps.title: Capture epifluorescence images
steps.instruction: Using an Olympus IX83 inverted epifluorescence microscope with CellSens Dimensions software (v3.1), collect Z‑stack images for each ring at a total thickness of 100 µm with a 2 µm step size; optimize exposure times based on negative controls (no primary antibody).

steps.title: Generate 2D projections
steps.instruction: In FIJI, apply the Extended Depth of Field plugin to project the 3D Z‑stacks into 2D images.

steps.title: Quantify vascular growth
steps.instruction: Save the projected images as false‑color JPEG files, then analyze them with AngioTool to calculate total vessel area and average vessel length per image.

steps.title: Assess stem marker colocalization
steps.instruction: Use the Just Another Colocalization Plugin (JaCoP) in FIJI to compute Pearson’s correlation coefficient between BON cell markers and stem‑cell markers.

steps.title: Analyze data statistically
steps.instruction: Export quantitative data and analyze with GraphPad Prism (v9) for indirect co‑culture or Excel with Real Statistics Add‑in (v7.6) for direct co‑culture; apply two‑sided t‑tests with equal variance or ANOVA with Bonferroni post‑hoc (α = 0.05), report mean ± SEM, and denote significance as * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001.

description: Overall Objectives: This protocol includes two different in vitro methods to co-culture cancer cells and vascular ECs. The first method is an indirect co-culture by transwell; our discussion of the protocol includes how to optimize concentrations of and ratios between cell types to study changes in cancer stem-like cell markers in cancer cell lines. The second method is a direct co-culture by the vasculogenic ring assay, in which cells are embedded in a disk-shaped ECM-based gel. To accomplish this, users fabricate poly(dimethylsiloxane) (PDMS) rings by using concentric core punches on a thin sheet of PDMS. The ring attaches to a glass coverslip; ultimately, this 3D model provides a highly rigorous and repeatable geometry for the 3D in vitro models to eliminate geometrical aberrations in casting the ECM-based gels. The assay is referred to as the vasculogenic ring assay, based on its origination to look at vascular growth and the ring-based geometry.1 The indirect protocol permits investigation of secreted factors from ECs on the regulation of stemness markers in cancer cells. While the methodology is fairly well established, the analysis of stemness markers in various types of cancer cells shows trends in stemness regulation based solely on ligand signaling. In contrast, the direct co-culture method provides an enhanced model of the tumor microenvironment (TME) where stromal components are adjacent to cancer cells, permitting investigations of juxtracrine signaling through ligand and cell-cell contact pathways. Comparing indirect and direct co-culture models provides a more thorough investigation of regulation cancer cell stem markers. Our results show how the cancer stemness-related markers including CD44, CD36, and ALDH1A1 are differentially regulated in indirect vs. direct co-culture methods. Read carefully and prepare materials and reagents before starting the experiments. Cell Culture Selection: MCF-7 cells are human breast cancer cells positive for estrogen r
